QUESTION OF THE WEEK - Ahead of the RBA board meeting next
Tuesday, economists were surveyed on their interest rate
outlooks. Briefly, a rate cut is seen as still a good chance in
July, but beyond early August economists said the likelihood of
another cut would decline. The RBA can cut on any day of the
month it chooses, meaning that markets will be on alert next
week, but also after inflation and wages data are released at
the end of the month. For this reason while some saw the RBA on
hold until its meeting in August 5, others said they would not
be surprised if the bank acted earlier.
BALANCE OF GOODS AND SERVICES - Always a difficult one to forecast, reflected by the wide range of forecasts. Generally a

narrowing of the surplus is expected, with exports falling back a little after their eight percent rise in April. The balance has alternated between surplus and deficit over the last seven months. RETAIL TRADE - After two consecutive falls, a strong rebound is expected in the May figures. But a rise of 2.0 percent would only take retail spending back to the level of February, and would not necessarily indicate any great strength. A number of economists mentioned anecdotal evidence that a cold snap in May would boost the month's figures. Generally a rise near the median was not expected to dent the front end of the yield curve too much, especially as the market has already pulled back from its very bullish stance of last week. BUILDING APPROVALS - While consumer spending has come off the boil after a strong start to 1997, most analysts see the housing sector as one of the best performers this year. Approvals are generally expected to rise again in May after a 3.6 percent rise in April. If approvals do rise it will be the first time they have risen in consecutive months since February and March 1996. In fact from last July until April's 3.6 percent rise, the pattern had been for a large rise of 10 percent or more followed by two smaller falls. Those at the top end of forecasts were expecting the Olympic village to be included in the figures. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800 (c) Reuters Limited 1997
